title: Was slower growth caused by culture—or was culture also shaped by history and institutions?

elements.text: Was slower growth caused by culture—or was culture also shaped by history and institutions?
The assignment is our question, not our answer. We compare six cases and ask which explanations survive the exceptions.
Method: original group framework. Evidence boundaries follow Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8), McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107), and the approved project theory matrix.

Start with a pattern. Make the mechanism explicit.
Look for a challenging case. Change the explanation.

Not Africa versus Asia as two uniform blocs. Not a ranking of people.
A bounded comparison of histories, mechanisms and outcomes.

title: Different systems of rule

elements.text: The useful comparison is what rule organised, extracted and left behind—not an empire label treated as destiny.

Different mechanisms may coexist. None of these studies supplies a causal ranking of the six cases or demonstrates that colonial rule was beneficial overall.

Limit: councils are not synonymous with democracy (Bolt et al., 2025; Huillery, 2009).

Kohli (1994) stresses organisational lineage under Japanese rule. Haggard et al. (1997) stress coercion, unequal ownership, division, war and post-1961 change.
Limit: continuity is not an uncontested causal finding.
Institutions on paper are not inclusion.

A British–French contrast cannot explain these experiences.

title: Independence inventory

elements.text: Six dimensions, unequal evidence. Read each row as a dated context—not a score or a common-year ranking.

World Bank (1985, p. 18); Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5); Xenos (1970, p. 1); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); Kohli (1994); Haggard et al. (1997); Asadullah et al. (2024, pp. 13–15); Dolan (1993), partial archival check.

Exports: cocoa dependence. Industry: import–export orientation. Skills: education base. Bureaucracy: not matched. Borders: independence territory, not a 1960 “culture” unit. Infrastructure: roads, rail; Tema under construction.
Exports: agriculture/cattle context; diamonds followed independence. Industry and infrastructure: very limited base. Skills: severe shortage. Bureaucracy: not matched. Borders: former protectorate.

Exports: sugar dependence. Industry: sugar-centred. Skills and bureaucracy: no matched independence metric. Borders: island state. Infrastructure: no matched inventory. Later diversification is not an inherited condition.

Exports and industry: colonial inheritance disrupted by division and war. Skills and bureaucracy: contested continuity. Borders: division is fundamental. Infrastructure: disruption; no matched common-year stock.

Exports: commodity-oriented inheritance. Industry: later electronics is not a starting asset. Skills: segmented opportunities. Bureaucracy: not matched. Borders: Malaya ≠ later federation. Infrastructure: no matched inventory.

Exports: agricultural orientation. Industry: no matched independence stock. Skills and bureaucracy: education and formal institutions alongside elite concentration. Borders/infrastructure: no matched inventory. Archival recheck pending.

title: How industrial capability compounds

elements.text: A conditional learning sequence—not an automatic cycle and not a recipe that travels unchanged.
World Bank (1993, pp. 4–7, 20–26, 79–80, 127–130, 159–161); World Bank (2020, pp. 32–33, Box 2 pp. 44–47). Original editorial synthesis of approved mechanisms.
These links do not isolate a single cause. External access, distribution, resources, institutions and political choices change the sequence and its effects.
People learn to absorb and improve production.
Capabilities need organisations and domestic links.
Standards, routines and coordination are tested.
Markets can bring scale, technology and feedback.
Returns must build new skills—not just protect rents.
Learning feeds back; links can break.
BREAK POINTS: unreliable services · weak feedback · imported inputs without local learning · protected failure. External conditions shape every link.

Domestic activity, but not the whole product value.
Transport, design and business services also matter.

title: Capability built over time

elements.text: South Korea’s sequence combined recovery, coordinated investment, performance pressure and learning. It also contained costly mistakes.
World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26, 127–130, 159–161, 242). Interpretive dispute: Rodrik (1995), investment-coordination argument (registered working-paper abstract, not a page-specific causal estimate).
The sequence is multi-causal. It does not establish culture as the cause or mean that another country can copy the same national model or international setting.
Recovery, agricultural change, education and infrastructure shaped the capacity to industrialise.
Credit and investment coordination accompanied export incentives and performance pressure.
Heavy and chemical industry expanded; policy also generated pressures, debt and bottlenecks.
Adjustment and liberalisation accompanied deeper firm learning and technological upgrading.

Durable direction mattered only if institutions could
learn from failure and change what was not working.

title: Six dimensions, one warning label

elements.text: National averages are historical, country-level lenses—not individual personalities, timeless truths or causal scores.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8 and 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 93–107). Definitions paraphrased, not reproduced. No country scores invented; missing country rows are not replaced with regional averages.

Acceptance of unequal power. Tested only as a conditional mechanism.
Integration into groups and obligations to them. Not a trust score. Conditional lens.
Achievement and competition versus care and quality of life; historically gendered labels. Context only.
Responses to ambiguity and uncertainty—not simply willingness to take risks. Context only.
Future-oriented adaptation and perseverance versus present/past obligations. Not policy duration. Conditional lens.
Social regulation of gratification. Not a measure of work ethic. Context only.

title: How far can trust travel?

elements.text: The target matters. A response about a bank, a neighbour or “most people” is not the same observation.

There is no approved common six-country trust scale here. Contemporary responses cannot be back-cast to 1960 or used alone to explain national growth.
A judgement about other people; a familiar person and “most people” are different targets.
Cooperation with known ties; not automatically the opposite of wider cooperation.
Trust in courts, banks or government must name the institution and the question.
Institutional-performance indicators are not measures of interpersonal trust.
Question wording, year, population, weights and context shape the reported measure.

Radius of Trust asks about cooperation beyond close ties.
The present evidence cannot establish its strong causal form.

elements.text: A network can be a source of resilience and a boundary on cooperation. Neither outcome follows automatically from “collectivism”.

Credit, labour, mutual help, survival and resilience when formal systems are absent or costly.
Delegation to unfamiliar people and impersonal scaling may become harder—depending on organisations and enforcement.

title: Authority, time horizons and missing evidence

elements.text: Authority, time horizons and missing evidence
Test power distance and long-term orientation as conditional mechanisms. Keep unsupported growth stories closed.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 9–16); McSweeney (2002, pp. 101–107); approved Hofstede critique pack and THEORY_EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md. No dimension is treated as a causal score.
National cultural measures cannot substitute for observed organisational behaviour, policy duration, investment or feedback. Mechanisms need their own evidence.
Hierarchy may organise action, but it may also weaken feedback. Test who can challenge decisions and whether errors are corrected.
Long-term orientation is not a policy-duration measure. Test observed investment, learning and correction over time.
Reopen with a specified direction, observed behaviour and matched timing—not a generic risk-taking story.
Reopen with a valid contemporary measure, a clear mechanism and tests against institutional and economic alternatives.
Reopen with a direct, timed link to saving or investment. Do not infer work ethic from income outcomes.

title: Connected Development

elements.text: What if the decisive difference was not how much infrastructure existed, but whom it connected?
World Bank (1993, pp. 20–26); World Bank (2020, Box 2, pp. 44–47); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8); Maipose (2008, pp. 3–5, 8–11); Nasution (2000, pp. 19–20). Original group hypothesis.
Connection alone neither establishes causality nor guarantees diversification. Investment, skills, institutions, resources and market access are bundled alternatives.
South Korea, Malaysia and Mauritius fit a productive-network account: skills, firms, infrastructure and market access worked together.
Botswana’s income gains challenge inherited infrastructure as a prerequisite. Mineral rents and institutions complicate the network story.
The Philippines shows that global connection can coexist with shallow domestic linkages. Export access is not the same as domestic learning.
Revise to the measured channel. Reject the causal ordering if deeper networks followed upgrading rather than preceding it.

title: Radius of Trust

elements.text: How far beyond family and close networks can economic cooperation scale?
OECD (2017, pp. 41–44, 62–79); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 12); approved trust evidence pack and six-country theory matrix. WGI is retained only as governance context.
The project cannot show that generalized trust caused firm scale or national growth. Governance indicators cannot close direct-trust gaps.
Institutions and organisations may extend cooperation beyond close networks. Contracts, firms and other arrangements may substitute for personal familiarity.
Direct trust measures differ by target, question and year. Ghana and South Korea remain direct-trust gaps. There is no harmonised historical six-country test.

Do not turn an evidence gap
into a cultural verdict.
REOPEN ONLY WITH comparable, weighted trust measures linked in time to firm-scale outcomes—and tests net of institutional substitutes.

title: Continuity + Adaptation

elements.text: Can a country learn industrially if direction changes every few years—and can continuity correct failure?
World Bank (1993, pp. 127–130, 159–161, 242); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014, pp. 5–8, 17); World Bank (2020, Box 2); approved theory matrix for Malaysia and the Philippines. Maipose (2008, pp. 8–11).
Cases cannot isolate duration from state capacity, mineral rents, FDI, market access, shocks or prior success. Hofstede long-term orientation is not a duration measure.
South Korea, Mauritius, Malaysia and the Philippines are consistent with durable direction plus feedback, learning and adaptation.
Stable policy may protect weak firms or ineffective programmes. Continuing the same failure is not industrial learning.
Accumulation without broad diversification is a warning—not a direct policy-duration test. Resources and institutional choices remain central.
Revise if continuity yields accumulation without variety; reject a strong claim when durable direction repeatedly preserves failure.

title: What the combined evidence says

elements.text: The strongest bounded explanation centres on productive capability—not fixed regional culture.
Original group synthesis of approved theory matrix and evidence packs. World Bank (1993, pp. 4–7, 20–26, 79–80); World Bank (2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); Hofstede (2011).
This is a bounded comparative interpretation, not an estimated causal decomposition. The six cases cannot represent every African or Asian economy.

History · institutions · resources · markets · policy
external conditions · culture

Divergence depended less on fixed regional culture than on whether states, firms, workers and external partners built and disciplined productive capabilities over time. Education, agricultural change, infrastructure, investment coordination, technology access and exports mattered in different sequences. Their effects depended on institutions, resources, distribution, history and international conditions. Culture may influence coordination, legitimacy and organisational practice, but it is not a stand-alone explanation.

sources: Original group synthesis of approved theory matrix and evidence packs. World Bank (1993, pp. 4–7, 20–26, 79–80); World Bank (2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); Hofstede (2011).

title: What can travel—and what must adapt?

elements.text: What can travel—and what must adapt?
Lessons are conditional mechanisms to examine, not national models to transplant.

Original group conclusions grounded in the approved theory matrix: World Bank (1993, 2020); Maipose (2008); Svirydzenka and Petri (2014); OECD (2017). These are reasoned implications, not independently identified causal effects.
Not only visible infrastructure. Ask whether people and firms can use it reliably and learn.
Link suppliers, workers, skills and markets—not just a port to the world.
Keep a direction long enough to learn; change policies that protect failure.
Use institutions and organisations; do not assume national trust scores explain growth.
Resources, history, scale and international conditions shape what is feasible.

Transfer mechanisms, not myths.
Adapt lessons, not entire national models.

title: If culture matters, can culture change?

elements.text: If culture matters, can culture change?
The final question returns us to the first: culture may shape economic organisation—and also change with institutions, opportunities and experience.
Hofstede (2011, pp. 6–8, 16); Beugelsdijk and Welzel (2018, pp. 1469–1475, Figures 7–9). Essential references continue on p. 26; image credits on p. 27.

Do not confuse a
historical pattern
with a permanent
national personality.

Culture is neither irrelevant nor sufficient. Cohort and historical change challenge a timeless reading of national averages (Beugelsdijk & Welzel, 2018). Our next question should name a mechanism, a context and evidence that could change our minds.

title: Images, data and open gates

elements.text: Every photograph has a country, place and date. Images provide context and human scale—not proof of culture, trust, productivity or causality.
